title: Skill issue (My OWN).
author: Aspiring_Serf
selftext:
Can any if you give any tips for how to make games look better? I get it's vague, but that's kind of the point. I just know I don't know enough to ask the right questions. I've always never been good at art or aesthetics and I usually a form over function guy, but I get games are also visual. I'm not looking for amazing graphics, but a way to make consistent, reliable, intuitive graphics and UI. I have read some things about design, and I've even loaded soem skills, but it's simply a thing I don't quite graph and "prompting harder" doesn't seem to be the answer. I'm basically building an excel sheet simulator (due to my actual skills and also lack of art), but making a pretty "Excel" and also any kind of game art to go with it is hard. I can provide examples, but not sure how helpful it would be as this is more about how to improve myself rather than a specific asset or screen.

TLDR, how do you "get good" at UI / UX when it jsir doesn't click for you?

comments.author: FlashMcSuave
comments.body: You need a style of your own, but you *also* need to use a lot of reference images. Find other things that look how you want yours to look, and take some aspects of them with you.

replies.author: selfish_meme
replies.body: But make sure all the refs have a consistent style like pairing a stylised character with an ultra real background is only going to work if that's your 'whole' style

comments.author: Quirky-Map1995
comments.body: My advice to get better at working with AI is to actually learn and try to understand how games are developed and then setup ur prompts according to what you working on narrow things down when polishing stuff and make general md that you update during the proccess to keep ur work consistent so you AI dont try to "reinvent wheel" anytime its making same proccess but rather just follow your workflow, many people think its just about giving "best prompt" but game developmnent with AI is great at utilizing and layering stuff that game engines and shaders already offer, you just need to give it good direction and for that you need to understand what is your goal with each step.

comments.author: klumpp
comments.body: What did you research about design? There are plenty of books about designing ui for more technical people. Forget prompts for a while and figure out what you want first.

replies.author: Aspiring_Serf
replies.body: Older books, mostly for html, and also watch a handful of game dev videos specifically about UI. I get it's not the deepest research, but it felt more and more like some basic rules such as fonts, and hit spots on screens and the rest was just "vibes and what looks good". Part of the issue is for example they will talk about framing in photography for example, and I get the rule, but not the why. And I will see people that tear down UI and say it's trash and I don't get why even after they explain it lol

comments.author: VG_Crimson
comments.body:
For me UX/UI is about 2 main things first and foremost:

1. Clarity at a glance
2. Convenience 

And secondary to that is presentation/style/aesthetics. 

Having a master level execution requires marrying all elements with each other, UX/UI that is clear and easy to understand at a mere glance and thus it is convenient to navigate and is stylish/pleasing to the eye whilst navigating. 

If there is friction in using it or reading it, in any amount, that's like a point taken off. Take off enough points and people start complaining and saying it's bad. But this is a granular issue where personal taste does affect your outlook on it. 

Therefore, you can't really make a "perfect" UX/UI but you can get somewhere close.

You have to begin with asking yourself what's needed from what you are making and why you are making it in the first place. Nail the function before you even dare think about the form. And make sure that form doesn't step on function's tail. It should never get in the way of gameplay.

replies.author: Aspiring_Serf
replies.body: Super helpful and your reward is a dumb followup question. If I am building a complex game, how do I not nerf depth, but also don't just give them walls of text. For example I'm trying to build a historically plausible colony sim. So actual grain yields, actual wages, crop rotation, indentured cargo costs, etc. I think economies and interactions are interesting ( fully get this will not be a commercial success game), but if someone wants that kind of game I don't want them to immediately be overwhelmed, analysis paralysis, or have systems they can't find and explore. I assume it's better to simplify the mechanics and get most of the depth out of the way if the player, but even that seems like something much easier said than done.

replies.author: VG_Crimson
replies.body:
There are work arounds, including something that might be a bit controversial. 

First the controversial point, look at examples of existing POPULAR games whose already pre-trained gamers how to read a certain layout. For my game the Dark Souls menu and Elden Ring menu is likely what I'll need to show off certain elements like affinities and damages and the like. I think it's not really a good design from the function perspective, but its burned into the minds of many at this point I would be foolish not to utilize that familiarity to some extent.That's one way tackle a complex system. 

The other advice I have is more traditional, but you should hide the complexity where it's not required to be known at that specific point in the navigation of UX/UI. There's no shame in not telling the players everything through the UI. In fact, hiding certain things from visibility could be in its own way a form of depth. A system underneath the game's surface they could only figure out by playing and paying attention. 

But for your highly specific case, I would look to other tycoon-esque games where you play from a "God-View" perspective. Take apart how they executed it and what you hated about it, what you liked about it. Chances are your audience has also played those types of games. 

IMO the only immediate way I can think of is to break that wall of text to Chunks given to the player only at the point in time in which they are relevant and in play, rather than all at once. You have to figure out what parts of your game are completely unreasonable to figure out without a prompt, what are slightly more reasonable for them to have picked up by just playing, and what is a given if they just paid attention. Prioritize what is absolutely key first, then you can prompt for details later. No shame in tutorialling the same thing twice from a different angle. People learn complex things over time after all and it's never a one and done deal with learning.

replies.author: BaseballRelevant4149
replies.body:
Tool tips with links. Every complex game is x10 better with tool tips with links.

Every resource, every mechanic, every location, everything gets a highlighted tool tip the player can hover their mouse over to get a brief explanation for what it is and how it works. Then if they want to know more they can click on it to take them to the menu its in and/or highlight the part of the UI its on. It's a 24/7 tutorial that stays out of the way until the player needs it.

It doesn't replace a well built UI but when a game gets complex enough that it needs menus within menus then tool tips with links are a must.

comments.body: When working on my stuff, I have the agent come up with an actual art style. It’s hold at taking design notes and sticking to them. I’ll usually feed it ideas and have it iterate until it’s making things that look consistent then tell it to always make things with these design decisions unless otherwise stated.

comments.author: 2ko2ko2
comments.body:
Probably just need to consume more media? I dunno. For me, even though I suck at art (I can draw but like... not good lol), I know exactly what I like because I have just consumed so much media that I have a good sense of "didn't like this for X,Y and Z reason" and "I loved this because of A, B and C". According to the sites I use to track stats, I have about 350 games played, 250 anime watched and 174 manga read. 

  
And when I consumed most of that, I consumed it critically. When I am playing a game I think about what I like and don't like, and WHY. Why is the important part I think in developing a taste, which will help guide you to a cohesive visual style. This is the biggest pitfall I see in a lot of aigames: they let the AI do all the artwork with prompts like: A cheerful girl smiling and laughing, with both arms in the air as she jumps up in the air". The AI has nothing to go off of in terms of what its supposed to look like. What's the framing? The color saturation? Is it supposed to be in a particular style like Anime? If so what kind of anime? Ghibli? Studio Trigger? 90's anime aesthetic? What's she wearing? So on and so on. Without all that direction, the AI will decide, and the AI can't actually think it just goes off of the data it has available. And when you just say "anime girl", it'll make an anime girl that looks like every other anime girl that the AI has ever designed. 

For me I think of a very specific feeling I want to capture. So if it's a 90's anime aesthetic, I think about "What do I like about that aesthetic? Which series can I point to that capture the feeling I am trying to capture?". I don't plan on using AI for my game but I have used them before (including my own local model with my own trained LoRAs), and the more context (and better yet, references) to the exact look you want, the better the result. 

Aside from just knowing exactly what you want through having a broad exposure to art in general, knowing your limits is the second part of making a game look good imo. It's one thing to say "I know exactly what I want, I want to build a game that takes from Cyberpunk 2077", and it's another to actually build a game that looks like Cyberpunk 2077. AI just isn't good enough to do it on its own. So do you have the skills to manually do what the AI can't? Have you designed a full world with a cohesive Cyberpunk aesthetic before? Can you spot bad topology and mesh in a 3D asset and fix them? If not, then maybe that isn't a good direction to take. For me, I want to make an RPG farming game with art inspired by Akira Toriyama (Dragon Quest, Dragon Ball), but I know for a fact I couldn't do it justice. I've used programs like PixelLabs and current models, and I know that even though it can make decent static images (if you know what you are doing) it's not great at doing smooth and dynamic animations. And I know I don't have the skills to fix it, so that idea is on the backburner until either AI is able to do what I want or my skills improve so I can do it myself. For now I'm working on a different game with a different aesthetic. I plan to use a manga aesthetic inspired by Inio Asano, blending digital photography of real places for backgrounds mixed with manga style characters. That I know I can do, especially with the help of AI if I find my skills can't (though I do want to try without the help of AI first. Not only to see if I can do it, but also I just think it allows me to put more of my own expression into the game). 

I see so many 3D games made by people with no experience with 3D modeling that look horrible, Build up your skills in 3D with small projects until you are ready if you don't have the skills yet, or pick a style you are confident you can pull off at your current skill level if you don't want to wait.

replies.author: 2ko2ko2
replies.body:
Yeah. There is a point of view by some creators that actually you shouldn't consume more media, because then you can only copy you cannot create. Miyamoto famously wasn't a gamer or programmer, but wanted to create manga. He pulled most of his ideas from his own life growing up. Many of those early pioneers at Nintendo did the same thing, pulling from their personal life.

*"Almost all Japanese animation is produced with hardly any basis taken from observing real people, you know. It's produced by humans who can't stand looking at other humans. And that's why the industry is full of otaku!"* is a famous quote from Ghibli's Miyazaki. He hates watching anime despite being possibly the world's most famous anime director.

The basic concept remains the same though. You chase a feeling. Zelda's design came from Miyamoto's childhood growing up in rural Japan and going on adventures in the mountains. The design of Pokemon came from Satoshi Tajiri's favorite childhood activity of collecting bugs. I think that visual design can also follow this pattern. Maybe you want to capture the look and vibe of your childhood neighborhood. Or the look and feeling of your favorite vacation spot. Miyazaki pulled designs from real Japanese architecture and folklore, maybe you want to go for a medieval  france aesthetic.

I think both ways are valid personally. Whether you look for inspiration from other works or from real life I think doesn't matter. What matters is that you think critically about what you want to capture, the feeling, and what about it gives it that feeling.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
UI/UX is a subject you can study and do research on. there are books/articles/blogs you can read etc

some people's full time job is literally just UI/UX so the rabbit hole is quite deep.

so no, it is some mystical knowledge that "clicks" with some people. you have to learn that stuff

if you dont want to be creative, you can always just copy other games' UI/UX

for example, your players shouldn't complain if you have a genshin impact style UI... that falls under the "acceptable" category for most gamers
